title: The water cycle
summary: Grade 5 students learn how water moves through evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection. They build a water cycle model in a bag, then finish with a labeled diagram and a paragraph tracing one water drop.
brief: The water cycle for grade 5 science: five 50-minute lessons. Follow my attached notes. Students explain evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection, build a water cycle model, and finish with a labeled diagram and a paragraph tracing one water drop. Grading: the diagram and paragraph 70%, lesson quizzes 30%. Support my two below-grade readers and the Spanish-speaking newcomer in every lesson with picture word banks, sentence frames and the key terms in Spanish.
policies:
Science notebooks stay in class; bring a pencil every day.

The kettle and the lamp are for the teacher only. Water on the floor is wiped up at once, and the lamp and its cord stay dry.

Lesson quizzes are taken alone with notebooks closed; the picture word bank and Spanish key terms stay out. A student who is absent takes the quiz on the day they return.

The final diagram and paragraph may use the word bank and sentence frames; Spanish labels beside the English ones are welcome.

l_fe746fa5d8e5.title: Water on the move: the big picture
l_fe746fa5d8e5.summary: Students see that water is always moving and changing, and start the water cycle bag on the sunny window to watch over several days.

segments.title: Where did the puddle go?
segments.description:
Show a photo of a puddle in a Phoenix parking lot after a monsoon storm, then the same spot at noon the next day, dry.
Students write one sentence with the frame: “I think the water went ___.”
They share with a partner, and the teacher collects three ideas on the board.
Set a clear glass of ice water on the front table now, for the demonstration in the next segment.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected ideas: soaked into the ground, went into the air, the sun dried it. Accept all; do not correct yet. Give the two below-grade readers the photo captions read aloud. Give the newcomer the picture word bank with agua, charco, aire, sol.

segments.title: Solid, liquid, gas
segments.description:
Hold up an ice cube, a cup of water and an empty cup. Explain that water is a solid as ice, a liquid as water and a gas as water vapor, which is invisible.
Show fresh droplets on the outside of the ice-water glass from the warm-up. Explain that vapor in the air turned into tiny drops of liquid on the cold glass, and the glass does not leak.
The teacher heats a fresh kettle just before this segment and holds a cold metal spoon in the white cloud above the spout, so students see new droplets form on the spoon. Point out that the clear space near the spout is vapor and the white cloud is droplets.
Students copy three words with a picture and Spanish term each: sólido, líquido, gas.
segments.teacherNotes:
Misconception: the white cloud is a gas. The cloud you can see is liquid droplets; the vapor is the clear gap by the spout. Do not reuse a kettle boiled earlier: it stops clouding. If it fails, the ice-water glass is the backup.
Safety: Teacher only handles the kettle. Boil it fresh on a stable table, students at least six feet back. The hot vapor and the cloud can burn, so use an oven mitt and tongs for the spoon. Unplug it and let it cool before moving or emptying. Wipe spills at once.

segments.title: The four stages
segments.description:
Use a large poster with pictures. Name the four stages and give each one a hand motion: evaporation (hands rise), condensation (fingers squeeze together), precipitation (fingers fall), collection (hands gather in a bowl).
Tell the story of a summer monsoon storm over Phoenix, following one drop from the clouds to a wash and back into the sky.
Students repeat the stage names with the motions and the Spanish terms: evaporación, condensación, precipitación, recolección.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep this as a big-picture preview; each stage gets its own lesson later in the course. Students may think the cycle starts at the ocean or at the clouds. Say it has no start, and any drop can enter anywhere. Sentence frame on the poster: “The water goes from ___ to ___.”

segments.title: Sort the water
segments.description:
In pairs, students get picture cards showing water in different places.
They sort the cards into three piles: solid, liquid, gas.
Pairs use the frame “This is a ___ because ___” to explain one card to another pair.
The teacher circulates and listens for the word vapor.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cards and expected piles, one per line:
Icicle on a roof: solid
Glass of tap water: liquid
Water vapor in the dry Phoenix air: gas
Hailstone: solid
River: liquid
Water vapor above a boiling pot: gas
Pair a below-grade reader with a partner who reads the labels aloud. The newcomer sorts by picture first, then adds Spanish labels.

segments.title: Build the water cycle bag
segments.description:
Each pair labels a zip bag with names, pours in about a quarter cup of tap water and draws a marker line at the water level.
They leave some air space above the water, seal the bag fully and tape it to the sunny window.
Each student writes a prediction with the frame: “I think the bag will show ___ because ___.” Then they draw the bag with the waterline in their science notebook.
Show the teacher’s bag, set up earlier, to preview what students may see in the coming days.
segments.teacherNotes:
Droplets may appear today or on a later day, depending on sunlight and temperature. Students should record what they actually observe. Set up a demonstration bag at least a day ahead for the preview. Plan short window checks on later days. Common mistake: students predict the bag will leak.
Safety: Water only; no tasting. Seal bags fully, tape them well above the floor, and wipe spills at once to prevent slipping. Use marker on the bag only, with caps closed when not in use.

segments.title: Lesson quiz (graded)
segments.description:
Students take the graded quiz on their own.
Cover the stage poster and anything showing the order of the stages. The picture word bank with Spanish terms may stay in scrambled order.
Read the questions aloud to the two below-grade readers and the newcomer, who may also use the Spanish key terms.
Collect the quizzes to mark later.
segments.teacherNotes: Use this lesson’s five-question quiz. Each question is worth 2 points, 10 points in all. For the written answers, accept any wording that gives the idea; spelling does not count. The newcomer may answer in Spanish or tell you the answer aloud. Collect to mark later.

segments.title: Exit ticket and take-home
segments.description:
Students answer the ungraded exit ticket on a slip: “Which stage do you think the bag will show first? Finish: I think ___ because ___.”
Collect the slips at the door.
Before students leave, set the short ungraded step toward the labeled diagram and paragraph, and hand out the take-home page with the picture word bank, sentence frames and Spanish key terms.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected answer: evaporation or condensation, because the sun warms the water and the vapor cools on the bag. Any prediction with a reason counts. Read slips before next time to see who still mixes up the stages.

keyIdeas: Water is always moving and changing between solid, liquid and gas.
Water vapor is a gas you cannot see. Clouds contain tiny liquid water droplets, ice crystals or both. Fog and the droplets on a cold glass are liquid water.
The water cycle has four stages: evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection.
A model, like a water cycle bag, lets us watch a big process on a small scale over several days. A scientist makes a prediction first.

vocabulary.definition: The three forms water takes: solid (sólido), liquid (líquido) and gas (gas).
Water as an invisible gas in the air (vapor de agua).
The way water moves around Earth and changes form again and again (ciclo del agua).
Liquid water turns into water vapor when it warms (evaporación).
Water vapor cools and turns into tiny drops of liquid water (condensación).
Water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail (precipitación).
Water gathering in oceans, lakes, rivers, washes and the ground (recolección).
A small copy of something big that helps us study how it works (modelo).

study.overview: Water is always moving and changing. In this lesson you saw water as a solid, a liquid and a gas, and you met the four stages of the water cycle. You also set up a water cycle bag on the sunny window. Read this guide to remember the big ideas before you watch your bag over the next few days.

points.heading: Water can be a solid, a liquid or a gas
points.explanation: Water is a solid (sólido) as ice, a liquid (líquido) as water, and a gas as water vapor. Water vapor is invisible. You cannot see it, but it is in the air all around us, even in the dry Phoenix air. Fog, clouds and the droplets on a cold glass are not vapor. They are tiny drops of liquid water, and clouds can also hold ice crystals. Example: when the teacher held a cold spoon in the white cloud above the kettle, new droplets formed on the spoon. The clear space near the spout was vapor. The white cloud was tiny liquid droplets.

points.heading: The droplets on a cold glass come from the air
points.explanation: A glass of ice water gets wet on the outside, but the glass does not leak. Water vapor in the air touches the cold glass and turns into tiny drops of liquid water. This shows that water changes from one state to another all the time. Example: the ice-water glass on the front table had fresh droplets on its outside, even though the water inside stayed in the glass.

points.heading: The water cycle has four stages and no start
points.explanation: The four stages are evaporation (evaporación), condensation (condensación), precipitation (precipitación) and collection (recolección). Use your hand motions to remember them: hands rise, fingers squeeze together, fingers fall, hands gather in a bowl. The cycle has no start. A drop can enter at any stage. Use this frame to describe a step: “The water goes from ___ to ___.” Example: in a summer monsoon storm over Phoenix, a drop falls from a cloud, runs into a wash, and later goes back up into the sky. Each stage gets a closer look later in the course.

points.heading: A model lets us watch a big process up close
points.explanation: A water cycle bag is a model. It shows a big process on a small scale, so we can watch it over several days. Your bag has a marker line at the starting water level and some air space above the water. A scientist makes a prediction first, then records what really happens, even if it is different from the prediction. Droplets may show up today or on a later day, depending on sunlight and temperature. Example: use the frame “I think the bag will show ___ because ___,” then look at your bag each day and write what you actually see.

l_417134c1320b.title: Evaporation: liquid water becomes vapor
l_417134c1320b.summary: Students explain how heat from the sun turns liquid water into invisible vapor, using Phoenix puddles and a lamp-heated cup. A short graded quiz checks the lesson.

segments.title: Check the bag and the puddle
segments.description:
Pairs check the water cycle bag on the sunny window. They compare the water to their marker line and draw what they see.
Then they finish the frame: “The puddle went into the air because ___.”
Hand back the exit slips from last time.
segments.teacherNotes: Droplets may or may not show yet; accept what students really see. Slips show who still mixes up evaporation and condensation. Picture word bank with agua, charco, aire, calor for the newcomer; read the frame aloud to the two below-grade readers.

segments.title: Heat turns liquid into vapor
segments.description:
Wipe a thin damp stripe on the whiteboard with a well-wrung sponge and trace its edge in marker. Students watch it shrink while you explain that heat in the room turns liquid water into vapor, and the vapor mixes into the air.
Connect it to the Phoenix parking lot puddle: the sun gave the heat, so the water rose into the air as invisible vapor.
Students say it with the hand motion for evaporation and the words heat, liquid and vapor. They add calor and vapor to their Spanish term lists.
segments.teacherNotes: Wring the sponge hard and test it before class: a thin film shrinks in two or three minutes in dry classroom air, but a dripping stripe will not. Trace again to show the change. If part of the stripe is left when the segment ends, look again before the quiz. Misconception: the water disappeared. It became vapor, still in the air. Sentence frame on board: “Heat turns ___ water into ___.” Picture cards for calor, líquido, vapor.

segments.title: Predict and set up the two cups
segments.description:
Show two identical open clear cups. Pairs help fill each to the same depth, mark the water line, and measure it with a ruler.
Place one cup close to the lamp. Place the other nearby with a cardboard card standing between it and the lamp, so it is shaded but open on all sides.
Each student writes a prediction: “I think the ___ cup will lose water faster because ___.” Leave the cups set up for next time.
segments.teacherNotes:
Before class, test the real lamp and cup positions: hold the back of your hand at the cup spot for one minute; it should feel clearly warm. If not, adjust the setup within the lamp manufacturer’s required clearance, using only an approved bulb within its wattage rating. Keep the plastic cups and cardboard away from the hot bulb. Keep both cups on the same table, away from vents and fans. Plan for unchanged readings: record them as results.
Safety: Lamp bulbs get hot. Do not touch the bulb or let the cup touch it. Keep cords and outlets away from water. Wipe spills at once. Do not drink the water.

segments.title: Read the cups from earlier
segments.description:
Show a pair of cups prepared in the same way a day ahead: same open cups, same starting depth, one near the lamp and one shaded by a card. Students measure from the bottom of each cup to the current water surface with a ruler. They use the marker line to identify the starting depth.
They record starting depth, now depth and the change for each cup in a two-row table.
They compare with their prediction and say which cup lost more water.
segments.teacherNotes: Start the prepared cups early enough for hours of lamp time. Expected result: the lamp cup lost slightly more. If both read the same, write “no measurable difference” and say the lamp may be too weak or the time too short. Do not change the numbers. Newcomer: table headers in English and Spanish.

segments.title: Explain what happened
segments.description:
Pairs explain the cup results using heat, liquid and vapor and the frame “The water in the ___ cup became vapor because ___.”
The class explains why the puddle in the parking lot dried faster at noon than at dawn.
Each pair shares one sentence with another pair.
segments.teacherNotes: Listen for heat as the cause. Watch for “the water went away” and “the water leaked out”; ask “Where is it now?” If results were unclear, discuss what a fair test needs: equal start, same airflow, same time. Sentence frames and Spanish terms in front of the three students who need them.

Read the questions aloud to the two below-grade readers and the newcomer, who may use the picture word bank and Spanish key terms in scrambled order.
segments.teacherNotes: Use this lesson’s five-question quiz. Each question is worth 2 points, 10 points in all. For the written answers, accept any wording that gives the idea; spelling does not count. The newcomer may answer in Spanish or tell you the answer aloud. Collect to mark later.

segments.title: Take-home step
segments.description:
Before students leave, set the short ungraded step toward the labeled diagram and paragraph.
Hand out the take-home page with the picture word bank, sentence frames and Spanish key terms.
Remind students that the cups stay in place and the bag stays in the window for the next check.
segments.teacherNotes: Make sure the two below-grade readers and the newcomer each have the page and know what to do. Collect nothing today; look at it next time. Keep the cups out of reach of students overnight and unplug the lamp.

keyIdeas: Evaporation happens when heat turns liquid water into water vapor, a gas you cannot see.
More heat makes evaporation faster, so a cup of water warmed by a lamp or the sun should lose water faster than a shaded cup, if the heat is strong enough to matter.
Scientists predict first, then measure the height of the water surface from the bottom of the cup over time and record what they actually see, even when nothing changes.

vocabulary.definition: Energy that makes things warmer; heat from the sun or a lamp makes liquid water turn into vapor (calor).
How high the water reaches in a cup; we mark it with a line and measure it with a ruler (nivel del agua).
A place where something blocks the light and heat from the sun or a lamp (sombra).
To say what you think will happen before you test it, and why (predecir).

study.overview: Today you learned how water leaves puddles and cups and goes into the air. This is called evaporation. Heat turns liquid water into water vapor, a gas you cannot see. You tested this with two cups of water, one near a lamp and one shaded by a card. You made a prediction, measured the water, and wrote down what you really saw.

points.heading: Heat turns liquid water into vapor
points.explanation: Evaporation happens when heat turns liquid water into water vapor. Water vapor is a gas, so you cannot see it. It mixes into the air. The water did not just disappear. It is still around us, as vapor. Think of the wet stripe your teacher wiped on the whiteboard. The edge shrank because the heat in the room turned the liquid into vapor. Use this sentence frame: “Heat turns liquid water into vapor.” Key words in Spanish: heat (calor), liquid (líquido), vapor (vapor).

points.heading: More heat means faster evaporation
points.explanation: When water gets more heat, it evaporates faster. A puddle in a Phoenix parking lot dries faster at noon than at dawn because the sun gives more heat at noon. The same idea applies to your cups. A cup of water warmed by the lamp should lose water faster than a cup shaded by a card, if the heat is strong enough to matter. Both cups must start with the same amount of water and have the same airflow. That makes it a fair test. Try this frame: “The water in the ___ cup became vapor because ___.”

points.heading: Scientists predict, measure and record what they see
points.explanation: A scientist first makes a prediction, such as “I think the lamp cup will lose water faster because it gets more heat.” Then the scientist measures. You put a ruler at the bottom of the cup and read the height of the water surface. You wrote the starting depth, the depth now, and the change for each cup. Always write what you really see. Sometimes the numbers do not change. If both cups read the same, write “no measurable difference.” That is a real result. It might mean the lamp was too weak or the time was too short. Never change the numbers to match your prediction.

points.heading: Check your thinking about where the water went
points.explanation: Some people say “the water went away” or “the water leaked out.” Ask yourself, “Where is it now?” The water in an open cup does not leak through the cup or vanish. It becomes vapor and goes into the air. Do not mix this up with condensation, which you met in the first lesson and will study next. Evaporation is liquid water becoming vapor. Keep your cups and your bag in place, because you will check them again next time.

study.overview: Condensation is what happens when water vapor in the air cools and turns into tiny drops of liquid water. In this lesson you used a cup of ice water to see it happen. The drops on the outside of the cup did not come from inside the cup. They came from vapor that was already in the air. Evaporation and condensation are opposites, and you can tell them apart by asking whether the water is gaining heat or losing heat.

points.heading: Condensation: cool vapor turns into liquid droplets
points.explanation: Condensation happens when water vapor in the air cools and turns into tiny drops of liquid water. Water vapor is a gas, so you cannot see it. When it touches something cold, it loses heat and becomes liquid you can see. Remember the hand motion: fingers squeeze together as you say, “Cool vapor turns into liquid droplets.” Example: a cloud forms when rising warm air cools and its vapor turns into tiny droplets. Words in Spanish: cold (frío) and drops (gotas).

points.heading: The drops on a cold cup do not come from a leak
points.explanation: In the demo, you filled a dry cup with cold water and ice and dried the outside. After a few minutes, drops formed on the outside. The cup was not leaking. In the class demo, the water inside the cup was colored, but the drops on the outside were clear. That shows the drops did not come from inside the cup. Ask yourself, “Where was the water before?” It was in the air as vapor. The drops formed on the outside because that surface was cold. Use this sentence: “The drops formed on the outside because the cold surface cooled the vapor in the air.” The cold does not make new water. It changes vapor that was already there into liquid.

points.heading: Evaporation and condensation are opposites
points.explanation: Evaporation needs heat and turns liquid water into vapor. Condensation needs cooling and turns vapor into liquid water. Examples of evaporation: a wet swimsuit drying on a pool fence, or wet footprints fading on a sunny sidewalk. Examples of condensation: drops on the outside of a cold water bottle just out of the fridge, or drops on the inside of the water cycle bag near the top. Words in Spanish: heat (calor) and cold (frío).

points.heading: How to tell them apart
points.explanation: Ask one question: is the water gaining heat and becoming vapor, or losing heat and becoming liquid? If it is gaining heat and becoming vapor, it is evaporation. If it is losing heat and becoming liquid, it is condensation. Example: a wet sponge on a sunny windowsill dries out. The sun adds heat, and the water becomes vapor, so it is evaporation. Try the frame: “This is ___ because the water ___.” Keep watching the water cycle bag in the window. If you see droplets, say where they are: “I see droplets on the ___ of the bag.”

study.overview: Water does not stay in the sky. When the tiny droplets in a cloud join together and get too heavy, they fall. That is precipitation. The fallen water then gathers in new places. That is collection. A Phoenix monsoon storm shows every part of the water cycle in one story. Collected water keeps moving, so the cycle never stops.

points.heading: Precipitation: water falls from clouds
points.explanation: Precipitation is water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail. Inside a cloud, tiny droplets bump into each other and join. When they grow too heavy to stay up, they fall. A cloud is not a bag of water that tips over. Its water came from vapor that evaporated and then condensed. Rain is liquid water. Snow forms when the air is below freezing. Hail is balls of ice from strong storms. Example: snow can fall on the mountains in northern Arizona, but Phoenix mostly gets rain. Say it this way: “Heavy drops fall as rain, snow or hail.” Spanish words: rain (lluvia), snow (nieve), hail (granizo), cloud (nube).

points.heading: Collection: where fallen water ends up
points.explanation: Collection is where fallen water ends up. Rain on hard ground runs downhill as runoff. It flows into dry washes, then to rivers and lakes. Some of the water also soaks into the ground. All of this gathered water is collection. Example: during a Phoenix monsoon storm, rain runs down the street into a dry wash, and some of it soaks into the dirt. Try this frame: “Rain runs off and collects in ___.” In Spanish: collection (recolección). Safety: never play in or cross a wash during a storm, because flooding can come fast. Remember: “Turn around, don’t drown.”

points.heading: A monsoon storm tells the whole cycle
points.explanation: A Phoenix summer monsoon storm connects all four parts of the cycle. First, the sun heats puddles and wet ground, and water evaporates into vapor. Winds also bring moist air into Arizona. Next, the vapor cools high up and condenses into tiny droplets that form a dark cloud. Then the droplets join, grow heavy and fall as rain. Last, the rain collects in washes and soaks into the ground. Use this frame to tell a storm story: “First ___, then ___, so ___.” Use the cycle words evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection in your own sentences.

points.heading: Collected water keeps moving, and results count
points.explanation: Water does not stop moving once it collects. After the storm, the sun heats the water in the wash or a puddle, and it evaporates again. So the cycle keeps going. Ask yourself, “Where does the puddle go next?” This also helps with our bag model. A scientist compares what a model shows with what was predicted. Your bag may show few droplets or none, and a few days is a short time. A different result is still a real result. Use this frame: “My prediction was ___, and the bag showed ___.” Keep the bag sealed and in the window for the next check.

Next, the vapor cools and becomes a cloud droplet through condensation. Then, the droplet joins other droplets and falls as rain on a farm through precipitation. Finally, the water runs off into a creek and returns to the lake through collection. The sun can heat the water again, so the cycle continues.
Show the checklist: four stage labels, arrows, a title, and a paragraph in order with cycle terms.

keyIdeas: One water drop can be traced through all four stages: evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection. After collection, the sun heats the water and the cycle starts again.
A labeled diagram names every stage and uses arrows to show which way the water moves.
A good tracing paragraph tells the drop’s path in order. It uses time words (first, then, next, finally) and the cycle terms correctly.
Evaporation needs heat and turns liquid into vapor. Condensation needs cooling and turns vapor into liquid. Telling these two apart is the key to a correct path.
What the bag showed is evidence. A scientist reports the real result, even when it differs from the prediction.

vocabulary.definition: A drawing with labels and arrows that shows how something works (diagrama).
A word or short phrase written next to a part of a drawing to name it (etiqueta).
To follow something step by step from where it starts (seguir).

study.overview: Today you turned what the water cycle bag showed into a labeled diagram and a paragraph that traces one water drop. A good diagram and paragraph show all four stages in the right order and use the cycle words correctly. Read this guide again before you finish your take-home work.

points.heading: One drop travels through all four stages
points.explanation: Water does not stop moving. A drop goes through evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection, and then the sun heats the water and the cycle starts again. For example, a drop in Lake Michigan is heated by the summer sun and evaporates. The vapor cools and condenses into a cloud droplet. The droplet falls as rain on a farm, runs off into a creek, and is collected back in the lake. Your own drop can start in a different place, but it must go through all four stages.

points.heading: Evaporation needs heat and condensation needs cooling
points.explanation: These two stages are easy to mix up, so ask one question: is the water gaining heat or losing heat? If it gains heat, a liquid becomes vapor. That is evaporation. If it loses heat, vapor becomes liquid. That is condensation. Cold does not make new water. It changes vapor that is already in the air into tiny drops, like the drops on the outside of a cold glass. Check each label and sentence in your work with this question.

points.heading: A labeled diagram shows the stages and the direction
points.explanation: Your diagram needs a title, a label for each of the four stages, and arrows that show which way the water moves. The arrows should make a loop. For example, the arrow from the lake to the cloud is labeled evaporation, not condensation, because the water is gaining heat. You may also add one detail you saw in the bag, such as droplets or the marker line. If your bag showed only part of the cycle, that is still a real result.

points.heading: A good paragraph tells the path in order
points.explanation: Start with where your drop begins. Then use the time words first, then, next and finally to move through the stages in order. Use each cycle term correctly and say what heat or cooling does at each step. A sentence might read, First, heat from the sun changes the liquid water into vapor through evaporation. Finish by saying the sun can heat the water again, so the cycle continues. Read your paragraph to a partner and check it against the checklist: four stage labels, arrows, a title, and a paragraph in order with cycle terms. Your work is scored as Excellent, Good, Developing or Beginning.

t_8fd4d75f5133.prompt: Look at the puddle photos from a Phoenix parking lot: wet after a monsoon storm, dry at noon the next day. Where did the water go? Some of you think it soaked into the ground. Some think it went into the air. Some think the sun dried it. Pick the idea you find most convincing and give one reason. Then listen to a partner who picked a different idea. Could more than one idea be true at the same time?
followUps: What could we look for or test to find out whether the water went into the ground, into the air, or both? Push students to name something they could observe, not just guess.
Why might the same puddle dry faster on a hot, sunny parking lot than in a shady spot? Ask students to connect the sun to what happens to the water.
If some of the water went into the air, what do you think it looked like when it got there? Gently bring out that vapor is a gas you cannot see, without correcting earlier ideas yet.

t_ec18e07b3c9c.prompt: Scientists make a prediction before they start an experiment. Each of you will set up a water cycle bag, tape it to the sunny window and write what you think it will show. Some of you may predict that the bag will leak. Others may predict droplets will form on the bag. Which prediction do you think is more likely, and why? Is it a problem if your prediction turns out to be wrong? Talk with your partner, then share.
followUps: Where do you think any droplets would come from if the bag is sealed and no water can get in or out? Ask students to point to the water in the bag, the sun and the cool bag surface in their answers.
Why do we draw a marker line at the water level before we start? Ask what the line would let us notice later.
If your bag shows nothing on the first day, what should you write in your notebook? Discuss why recording what you actually see matters more than matching your prediction.

t_3229c730c287.title: Choose a water drop’s starting place
t_3229c730c287.prompt: At home, begin planning the path for one water drop in your final labeled diagram and paragraph. This is ungraded practice. You may ask someone at home to help you read or talk through your idea.
steps: Draw one place where water can collect, such as a birdbath or a puddle. Label it collection (recolección).
Add one water drop to your drawing. Write a prediction: “I think the drop could go next to ___ because ___.”

t_66fb2c31f661.prompt: Water in an ice cube tray has frozen. What state is the water in?
t_66fb2c31f661.explanation: Frozen water is a solid. Liquid water and water vapor are the other two states in this lesson.

t_b6d75c5ac8b6.prompt: A lake warms, water rises into the air as vapor, droplets form in clouds, rain falls, and water gathers in a pond. Which list names the stages in that order?
t_b6d75c5ac8b6.explanation: Evaporation changes liquid water to vapor, condensation forms droplets, precipitation brings water down, and collection is where water gathers.

t_ac80b0bce199.prompt: A pair wants to tell whether the water level in its sealed bag changes. What should the students do before taping the bag up, and why?
t_ac80b0bce199.answer: Draw a marker line at the water level so they can compare the level later.
t_ac80b0bce199.explanation: The line records the starting water level. Students can compare it with what they observe later.

t_033d95848776.prompt: A water drop can enter the water cycle at any stage because the cycle has no single starting point.
t_033d95848776.explanation: The cycle has no single start; a drop can enter it at any stage.

t_b4eb617d98f2.prompt: Before observing a sealed water cycle bag on a bright window, what makes a useful prediction?

choices.text: What the bag may show and a reason
What the bag will show and no reason
What the bag may show and a drawing
What the bag will show and a waterline

t_b4eb617d98f2.explanation: A prediction says what a student thinks may happen and gives a reason for that idea.

t_a733c84b0c13.prompt: A puddle in a Phoenix parking lot is gone by afternoon. One student says, “The water went away.” Another says, “The water is still here, but in the air.” Which statement do you agree with, and what evidence from today’s lesson could you use to convince someone who disagrees?
followUps: Where is the water now? How could we show that it did not just vanish, for example with the whiteboard stripe?
What words would you use to describe the water in the air: heat, liquid, vapor? Can you see it?
What would you say to a friend who thinks the puddle leaked into the ground?

t_6e83421d04b9.prompt: Before we read the cups, two students disagree. One says the cup near the lamp will lose more water. The other says both cups will lose the same amount because they are both open. Which prediction do you support, and why? What would you do if the numbers came out the same?
followUps: What is the cause you expect: what does the lamp give the water in the cup?
If both cups read the same, is that a failed test or a result? What could be too weak or too short?
What must stay equal in a fair test so we can trust the answer?

t_2bc73bb3568a.title: Add evaporation to your water drop’s path
t_2bc73bb3568a.prompt: At home, build on the starting place you chose for your water drop. Add one evaporation part to its path. This is ungraded practice for your final labeled diagram and paragraph. You may ask someone at home to help you read or talk through your idea.
steps: Draw an arrow from your starting place to show where the water goes during evaporation.
Label the liquid water, a source of heat, and the water vapor. You can use these Spanish terms: líquido, calor, vapor.
Complete: “Heat from ___ changes liquid water into ___.”

t_3265600482ad.prompt: During evaporation, heat changes liquid water into what?
t_3265600482ad.explanation: Evaporation happens when heat turns liquid water into water vapor, a gas that cannot be seen.

t_a1e74ca0b606.prompt: Two matching open cups start with the same amount of water. One sits on a sunny window ledge, and the other stays in a shaded spot. The sunny cup’s water gets warmer. Which cup should lose water faster?

choices.text: The shaded cup, because shade makes water warmer
The sunny cup, because its water gets more heat
Both cups, because heat does not affect evaporation
Neither cup, because open water cannot evaporate

t_a1e74ca0b606.explanation: More heat makes evaporation faster, so the warmer cup should lose water faster if the heat is strong enough to matter.

t_ad99ae35a60f.prompt: You measure a cup’s water surface from the bottom at two checks. Both readings are the same. What should you record?
t_ad99ae35a60f.answer: Record both measured heights and note that there was no change, or no measurable difference.
t_ad99ae35a60f.explanation: Scientists record what they actually measure, even when the water level does not change.

t_0e55fa9beba5.prompt: A cup’s water surface is 6.8 cm above the bottom at the starting check and 6.1 cm at the later check. How much did the water level decrease?
t_0e55fa9beba5.explanation: Subtract the later height from the starting height to find the decrease.

t_d504640d9acc.prompt: Two matching open cups start with the same water height. One is in sunlight near a fan, and one is shaded away from the fan. After the same amount of time, the sunny cup has a lower water level. What can you conclude?

choices.text: Heat alone caused the change in water level
Shade caused the sunny cup to lose water
The cups must have started at different heights
Different airflow means heat alone was not tested

t_d504640d9acc.explanation: A fair comparison keeps airflow the same. Since the cups had different airflow, the result cannot show that heat alone caused the difference.

t_145ae9e62769.prompt: A classmate says, “The cold glass leaks. The water on the outside came from inside.” Another says, “The drops came from the air.” Which claim do you believe, and what could you do or look for to test it? Be ready to change your mind if the evidence says so.
followUps: In the demo with colored water, what color were the drops on the outside? What does that tell us about whether they came from inside the cup?
Ask: “Where was the water before it was on the glass?” Press students to say it was in the air, as vapor.
What if the glass were warm instead of cold? Would drops still form on the outside? Why or why not?

t_0b6d5b1d348e.prompt: Evaporation and condensation are opposites. One student says, “They are the same thing, because both are about water and air.” Another says, “They are different.” Who is right? Use the cases of a wet sponge on a sunny windowsill and drops on a cold water bottle to argue your side.
followUps: In each case, is the water gaining heat or losing heat? How does that help you decide?
Is the water becoming vapor or becoming liquid in each case? Which word fits each one?
Use the frame: “This is ___ because the water ___.” Can a partner who disagrees use the same frame to give a different answer?

t_0fbd9295b43d.title: Add condensation to your water drop’s path
t_0fbd9295b43d.prompt: At home, build on the starting place and evaporation part you chose. Add condensation to your water drop’s path. This is ungraded practice for your final labeled diagram and paragraph. You may ask someone at home to help you read or talk through your idea.
steps: Choose a place where your water vapor could cool and become tiny liquid drops.
Add that part to your path with a small drawing or a few words.
Finish the frame: “The water vapor cooled and became ___.”
Use the picture word bank if it helps: air (aire), cold (frío), water vapor (vapor de agua), drops (gotas), condensation (condensación).

choices.text: Liquid water warms and becomes vapor
Liquid water cools and becomes solid ice
Water vapor warms and becomes liquid drops
Water vapor cools and becomes liquid drops

t_cf32b04fbff3.explanation: Condensation happens when water vapor cools and turns into liquid droplets.

t_65048cce1a3e.prompt: Drops that form on the dry outside of a cup of ice water come from water vapor in the air.
t_65048cce1a3e.explanation: The cold outside surface cooled water vapor in the air, forming drops there.

t_5051ed348687.prompt: A wet soccer jersey dries on a warm, breezy clothesline. Which process changes the liquid water in the jersey into vapor?
t_5051ed348687.explanation: The water gains heat and changes from liquid into vapor. That is evaporation.

t_5a2ff41dd59c.prompt: Which condition makes water vapor turn into liquid droplets?
t_5a2ff41dd59c.explanation: Cooling changes water vapor into liquid droplets through condensation.

t_2957a56cdaaf.prompt: A wet towel dries, and later some of its water vapor cools and forms liquid drops on a cool surface. Name the two processes in order. Explain what happens to the water in each process.
t_2957a56cdaaf.answer: Evaporation happens first: liquid water in the towel changes into vapor. Condensation happens next: the vapor cools and changes into liquid drops.
t_2957a56cdaaf.explanation: Evaporation changes liquid water into vapor; condensation changes cooled vapor into liquid droplets.

t_a816deaa930d.prompt: Your bag model shows only a few droplets, or none, after a few days. A classmate says, ‘The model failed, so it proves nothing.’ Another says, ‘A different result is still a real result.’ Which of you do you agree with, and why? Use what you predicted and what the bag showed.
followUps: What could be the reason the bag shows few droplets? Think about the sun, the heat and how many days have passed.
If a scientist’s prediction turns out different from the result, what could the scientist do next?
What would you change or keep the same if you checked the bag again later?

t_4d7e443b825c.prompt: A friend says, ‘A cloud is like a bag of water that tips over when it is full.’ Do you agree? Use a Phoenix monsoon storm to explain where the cloud’s water came from and what makes it fall. Then decide: once rain collects in a wash, does the water stop moving?
followUps: Where did the cloud’s water come from before it was in the cloud? Use the words evaporation and condensation.
What happens to the droplets inside a cloud before they fall as rain, snow or hail?
After the storm, where could the water in the wash go next? Use the sun in your answer.

t_029ed182b825.title: Add precipitation and collection to your water drop’s path
t_029ed182b825.prompt: This ungraded at-home practice builds on the starting place, evaporation, and condensation you already chose for your final labeled diagram and paragraph. Add what happens after the water drop reaches a cloud, then show where it goes. You may ask someone at home to help you read or talk through your idea.
steps: Choose whether your drop falls as rain, snow, or hail. Add precipitation to your path. Use the word bank: rain (lluvia), snow (nieve), hail (granizo), cloud (nube).
Show where the fallen water collects, such as in a wash, a river, a lake or the ground. Add collection (recolección) to your path.
Use these frames to explain your new part: “The water falls as ___.” “Then it collects in or on ___.”

t_6d1eeb6149fc.prompt: Inside a cloud, tiny water droplets bump together and grow. What happens when the drops become too heavy to stay up?

choices.text: The drops soak into the cloud as collection.
The drops turn into vapor by condensation.
The wind pushes the whole cloud downward.
The drops join and fall as precipitation.

t_6d1eeb6149fc.explanation: Precipitation happens when cloud droplets join, grow heavy, and fall as rain, snow, or hail.

t_3520baba74e0.prompt: Which sequence best describes how a Phoenix monsoon storm can connect parts of the water cycle?

choices.text: Rain collects first, the sun cools the ground, and clouds release vapor into the air.
Clouds form from runoff, rain evaporates, and the vapor soaks into the ground.
Wet ground releases vapor, vapor condenses into clouds, rain falls, and water collects.
Wet ground releases vapor, rain forms, clouds collect it, and the air turns into runoff.

t_3520baba74e0.explanation: The sun can warm wet ground so water evaporates. Vapor cools and condenses into clouds. Rain then falls and collects on or in the ground.

t_75977cd27355.prompt: A student predicts that the water line in a sealed bag will stay the same. After several sunny days, the line is lower and droplets are visible inside the bag. Which statement best compares the result with the prediction?

choices.text: The result matched; the water line stayed the same in the bag.
The result differed; water moved and droplets formed inside the bag.
The result differed; the bag made new water from the sunlight.
The result matched; the droplets show that water did not move.

t_75977cd27355.explanation: The observed lower water line and droplets differ from the prediction. Comparing a model’s result with a prediction helps describe what the model showed.

t_5cacb851cf94.prompt: A cloud is a bag of water that tips over to make rain.
t_5cacb851cf94.explanation: Cloud water comes from vapor that cooled and condensed into droplets. Drops can join and become heavy enough to fall as precipitation.

t_4fd5a77388db.prompt: During a Phoenix monsoon, rain falls on pavement and flows into a wash. Explain where the water collects and what the sun may cause some of it to do next.
t_4fd5a77388db.answer: The runoff collects in the wash. Later, the sun can heat some of the collected water so it evaporates again.
t_4fd5a77388db.explanation: Collection is where fallen water gathers, such as in a wash. Collected water keeps moving through the cycle and can evaporate again when heated by the sun.

t_598e98af2511.prompt: Imagine your bag showed only a few droplets, or none at all, but your diagram shows a full cycle with clouds and rain. Is that a problem? Should a scientist’s diagram show only what the bag showed, or the whole cycle? Argue for your side.
followUps: What did the bag show in your pair, and which stage did it show best? What stage could it not show in a short test?
If a scientist’s result is different from the prediction, what should the scientist do? Why is reporting the real result better than changing it?
Which would you trust more: a diagram of only what we saw, or a diagram of the whole cycle? What evidence would make you more sure about the missing stages?

t_57ff0d089331.prompt: A classmate writes: ‘The cold makes new water in the cloud.’ Do you agree? Decide whether the cold makes water or changes water that was already there. Then explain which stage in a drop’s path you are talking about, and what heat or cooling does there.
followUps: Where was the water just before it became a cloud droplet? What form was it in then?
Think of a cold glass of ice water with drops on the outside. Does the glass leak, or did the water come from somewhere else? How could you tell?
How would you fix the classmate’s sentence using the words evaporation or condensation, and the words heat or cooling?

t_fd69428605ef.title: Labeled diagram and paragraph
t_fd69428605ef.prompt: Show one possible path for a water drop through the water cycle. Finish the diagram and paragraph you started in class, using the starting place you chose. Make a labeled diagram and write one short paragraph of about 4–6 sentences that traces the drop through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection. Explain how heat or cooling changes the water. Use time words to show the order. This is the graded diagram and paragraph, worth 70% of the unit grade.
steps: Finish your diagram. Give it a title and show your drop’s path from its starting place through all four stages. Label each stage and use arrows to show the direction the water moves.
Finish your paragraph of about 4–6 sentences. Trace the drop in order, using time words such as first, then, next, and finally.
Use evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection correctly. Explain that heat changes liquid water into vapor and cooling changes vapor into liquid water.
Check that your diagram and paragraph tell the same path. Use the picture word bank, sentence frames, and Spanish key terms on your take-home page if they help.

t_a729ec9ac0e7.prompt: In a sunny place, liquid water changes into water vapor. Which stage is happening?
t_a729ec9ac0e7.explanation: Evaporation happens when heat changes liquid water into vapor.

t_73beb995dff7.prompt: In a water cycle bag, water vapor cools on the plastic and forms tiny liquid drops. Which stage do the drops show?

choices.text: Evaporation, when liquid water becomes vapor
Precipitation, when drops fall from a cloud
Collection, when water gathers in one place
Condensation, when vapor becomes liquid drops

t_73beb995dff7.explanation: Cooling changes water vapor into liquid drops. That process is condensation.

t_cedd13c56b0d.prompt: Which set of arrows shows water moving through the four stages and back to collection?
t_cedd13c56b0d.explanation: After water collects, heat can cause evaporation. Vapor cools through condensation, then water falls as precipitation and collects again.

t_52787b2c9b4d.prompt: On a labeled water cycle diagram, what should the arrows show?
t_52787b2c9b4d.answer: The direction water moves from one stage to the next.
t_52787b2c9b4d.explanation: Arrows show the water’s path through the cycle stages.

t_fa97aa7a1b18.prompt: A tracing paragraph tells the drop’s path in order and uses water cycle terms correctly.
t_fa97aa7a1b18.explanation: Time words and correct cycle terms help explain the drop’s path in order.

descriptors.x_453923b8d145: Gives little of the drop’s path, with few correct cycle terms.

f_802ee22f1bd0.question: Is the white cloud above the kettle water vapor?
f_802ee22f1bd0.answer: No. Water vapor is a gas, and you cannot see it. The white cloud is tiny drops of liquid water. The clear space near the spout is the vapor. The drops on the cold spoon and on the ice-water glass formed the same way: vapor met something cold and turned into liquid.

f_c213843bffd3.question: Why are there drops on the outside of the cold glass? Is the glass leaking?
f_c213843bffd3.answer: The glass does not leak. Water vapor in the air touched the cold glass and turned into tiny drops of liquid water. The water came from the air, not from inside the glass.

f_8bcd5d6d1f58.question: Where does the water cycle start?
f_8bcd5d6d1f58.answer: It has no start. Any drop of water can enter the cycle at any place. The four stages are evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection, and the water keeps moving through them again and again.

f_3b10b7d53041.question: Why do we make a prediction before we look at the water cycle bag?
f_3b10b7d53041.answer: A scientist makes a prediction first so there is something to test. You write what you think the bag will show and why. Then you record what you actually see on the window, even if it is different from your prediction. Droplets may show up today or on a later day. The marker line helps you see if the water level changes.

f_d9ac9c8365b7.question: Where does the water go when a puddle dries up?
f_d9ac9c8365b7.answer: Heat from the sun turns the liquid water into water vapor. Vapor is a gas you cannot see, and it mixes into the air. The water did not disappear. It is still in the air, just too small to see.

f_942a75298004.question: What if both cups show the same water level?
f_942a75298004.answer: Write “no measurable difference” and record the numbers you really measured. That is a real result. The lamp may be too weak or the time too short. Do not change the numbers to match your prediction.

f_53055933bccd.question: Is the cup leaking when water is gone, or when drops show on the outside of a cold glass?
f_53055933bccd.answer: No, the cup is not leaking. In an open cup, liquid water becomes vapor and goes into the air. Drops on the outside of a cold glass are a different thing: water vapor from the air turns into liquid on the cold glass. The next lesson looks at this closely.

f_0fff69189144.question: If the cup doesn’t leak, where does the water on the outside come from?
f_0fff69189144.answer: It comes from water vapor that was already in the air. The vapor touches the cold cup, cools, and turns into tiny drops of liquid water. The cold does not make new water. Ask yourself: where was the water before? It was in the air.

f_eae7d1be439e.question: Why do the drops form on the outside of the cup and not somewhere else?
f_eae7d1be439e.answer: The outside surface is cold, and air with vapor in it touches that surface. When the vapor loses heat, it turns into liquid. In our demo we dried the outside first, so any drops we saw there had to come from the air. Drops may also form on the inside above the water, but we focus on the outside.

f_9c3898ed5ec1.question: How can I tell evaporation from condensation?
f_9c3898ed5ec1.answer: Ask whether the water is gaining heat and becoming vapor, or losing heat and becoming liquid. Gaining heat and becoming vapor is evaporation, like wet footprints fading in the sun. Losing heat and becoming liquid is condensation, like drops on a cold water bottle. They are opposites.

f_317770e8cfec.question: Is a cloud a bag of water that tips over?
f_317770e8cfec.answer: No. A cloud is made of tiny droplets that formed when water vapor cooled and condensed. The droplets bump together and join. When they grow too heavy to stay up, they fall as rain, snow or hail. The cloud’s water first evaporated from places like wet ground and puddles.

f_b627a894a79e.question: Does water stop moving once it collects in a wash, river, lake or the ground?
f_b627a894a79e.answer: No. Collected water keeps moving. The sun heats it and some of it evaporates again, so the cycle keeps going. Water in a wash or a puddle after a monsoon storm is a good example. Some water also soaks into the ground.

f_3b8e817324f4.question: What if our bag model shows few droplets or none? Did we do it wrong?
f_3b8e817324f4.answer: No. A few days is a short time, so a bag may show little change. A scientist compares what the model shows with what was predicted. A different result is still a real result. Draw what you see and write it down. Keep the bag sealed and leave it in the window.

f_de8830ca4376.question: My bag has only a few droplets, or none. Did I do it wrong?
f_de8830ca4376.answer: No. A short test may show only part of the water cycle, and that is still a real result. Scientists report what they actually see, even when it is different from what they predicted. Write what your bag showed, then use the cycle stages to draw the whole path of your drop.

f_50ec0f291985.question: How do I know which stage to label evaporation and which to label condensation?
f_50ec0f291985.answer: Ask: is the water gaining heat or losing heat? Evaporation needs heat and turns liquid water into vapor. Condensation needs cooling and turns vapor into liquid droplets. Cooling does not make new water. It changes vapor that was already there back into liquid.

f_d19b0ba19f36.question: What should my paragraph include, and how does my drop’s path end?
f_d19b0ba19f36.answer: Tell your drop’s path in order, from its starting place through all four stages. Use time words such as first, then, next and finally, and use the cycle terms correctly. Say what heat or cooling does at each step. After collection, the sun can heat the water again, so the cycle continues. Check your work against the checklist before you hand it in.

# My notes for the water cycle unit

A grade 5 teacher’s own planning notes for this unit, written for this sample course.

- Last year students mixed up evaporation and condensation. The "cold glass of ice water" demo helped: droplets form on the outside, not because the glass leaks.
- We have a classroom kettle (teacher use only), clear plastic cups, plastic wrap, ice, a lamp, zip bags and markers.
- Our school is in Phoenix, Arizona: summer monsoon storms are a good local example; most students have never seen snow fall.
- I want a "water cycle in a bag" model taped to the sunny window, checked over several days.
- Students should finish with a labeled diagram and a short paragraph explaining one path a water drop could take.
- Two students read well below grade level; one is a newcomer who speaks Spanish.
